title: A giving review
hookLine: once a year, look at what you gave
tomorrow: why is it easier to be kind to strangers than at home?

cards: At the end of the year, the apps hand you a recap: your top songs, your steps, the places you went. Nobody sends a giving recap.

If one existed, it would show more than money: the hours, the rides, the meal dropped off, the few dollars for a friend's fundraiser. And it would show whether any of it was planned, or only leftover.
Jesus once sat and watched people give, and he did the math differently.

teach.b: At the Temple treasury, rich people put in large gifts. Then a poor widow drops in two small coins. Jesus calls his friends over: “this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury.”
They gave out of plenty, he says; she “of her want did cast in all that she had.” Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: the smallest gift in the story is the one Jesus points out.
He measured the cost to the giver, not the size.
In Luke he gives a rule of thumb: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.” Small, steady faithfulness is where the larger kind grows.
Paul adds the spirit of it: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Purposeth in his heart: giving here is decided, not just something that happens. He even suggests setting it aside “upon the first day of the week.” That's what a giving review is for.
Once a year, look back at what you gave: money, time, skill, attention.
Was it planned or leftover? Cheerful or grudging?
Christians answer how much in different ways; some aim for a tithe, some give as they're able, some give mostly time. The review isn't a scorecard. It's the heart deciding again.

how: Some Christians set a yearly time to look back at their giving of money, time and skill and adjust it; some aim for a tithe, a tenth, while others give as they're able or give mostly time.

games.q: your book club wants one big gift in December instead of small monthly ones. using Luke 16:10, make the case for small and steady.
o: small gifts don't matter; only the big one helps anyone.
faithful in the least grows into faithful in much; steady giving shapes the giver.

games.why: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." Paul even suggests setting something aside on the first day of the week.

practice: Count on your fingers what you gave this past year, and not only money: an afternoon, a ride, a listening ear, a skill. When your fingers run out, pick one you'd like to give again on purpose.
Hold that one through the rest of the sit.
